title: The story of Naciketas, told and heard
theme: The wise one who tells and who hears this ancient story of Naciketas, told by Death, is honoured in the world of Brahman.

words.context: Śaṅkara: the story of the three vallīs, «वल्लीत्रयलक्षणं»

sandhi.type: m before a vowel; m before a consonant
sandhi.rule: A final m before a vowel is kept and joined to it; before a consonant it becomes anusvāra, P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः).

morphology.note: A derivative of the name Naciketas with vṛddhi of the first syllable: ‘belonging to Naciketas’. The same form names the Nāciketa fire in 1.1.18 and 1.2.10; here it qualifies the story.
From the stem mahīya-, ‘be great, be honoured’, related to √mah; the ending is middle and the sense passive or intransitive.

translation.literal: Having told and having heard the ancient story of Naciketas, told by Death, the wise one is honoured in the world of Brahman.
translation.readable: The wise one who tells, or hears, this ancient story of Naciketas as Death told it is honoured in the world of Brahman.

anvaya: मेधावी मृत्युप्रोक्तम् सनातनम् नाचिकेतम् उपाख्यानम् उक्त्वा श्रुत्वा च ब्रह्मलोके महीयते ।
syntax: One sentence: the object (the story, with three adjectives) stands first, then two absolutives joined by ca, the subject medhāvī, the locative and the verb.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara takes the compound as ‘the world that is Brahman’, «ब्रह्मैव लोको ब्रह्मलोकः», and ‘is honoured’ as becoming one with it, the object of worship: «आत्मभूत उपास्यो भवतीत्यभिप्रायः». The phrase can also be read as the world of Brahmā; Raṅgarāmānuja's surviving comment does not discuss it.

Śaṅkara: ancient because it is Vedic, «चिरन्तनं वैदिकत्वात्». Raṅgarāmānuja: eternal as a stream, because it is not of human authorship, and Death only its speaker: «मृत्योः प्रवक्तृत्वमेव न स्वतन्त्रवक्तृत्वम्».

beginner: The first half of the Kaṭha is ending, and the text steps back to praise the story it has told. It calls it the story of Naciketas, as told by Death, and says it is ancient. A wise person who tells it to others, or hears it from a teacher, is honoured in the world of Brahman. Śaṅkara says the verse is there to praise the knowledge just taught, and he reads ‘the world of Brahman’ as Brahman itself: such a person becomes one with it. Raṅgarāmānuja adds that the story is ancient in a strong sense: it was not made up by anyone, not even by Death, who only passes it on. Verses like this one, and the next, are a traditional way of closing a section and inviting the hearer to keep the teaching alive.
analogy: Like a family story passed down for generations: no one remembers who first told it, and each telling keeps it alive.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It praises the story of Naciketas told by Death as ancient, and says that the wise one who tells or hears it is honoured in the world of Brahman.

commentary.q: Śaṅkara: praise of the knowledge taught
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The verse is spoken to praise the knowledge just taught: «प्रस्तुतविज्ञानस्तुत्यर्थमाह श्रुतिः». The story is the three vallīs, «वल्लीत्रयलक्षणं», ancient because Vedic; one tells it to brāhmaṇas and hears it from teachers. The world of Brahman is Brahman itself, and the wise one becomes one with it, the object of worship.

commentary.q: Raṅgarāmānuja: Death is only the speaker
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: He calls the verse a conclusion, «उपसंहरति». ‘Told by Death’ means Death is its speaker, not its author: «मृत्योः प्रवक्तृत्वमेव न स्वतन्त्रवक्तृत्वम्». So it is ancient, eternal as a stream, because it has no human author: «अपौरुषेयत्वात् प्रवाहरूपेण नित्यमित्यर्थः».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: This verse and the next close the first adhyāya (the first three vallīs); Śaṅkara's colophon after 1.3.17 marks its end. The commentaries used in this edition go on to comment on the second adhyāya as the same text.

advaita.text: Praise of the knowledge taught; the world of Brahman is Brahman itself, «ब्रह्मैव लोको ब्रह्मलोकः», with which the knower becomes one.

visistadvaita.text: The story is eternal and not of human authorship; Death only speaks it: «अपौरुषेयत्वात् प्रवाहरूपेण नित्यमित्यर्थः».

schools.disagreement: No real disagreement; Śaṅkara reads ‘the world of Brahman’ as Brahman itself, and Raṅgarāmānuja's comment does not address the phrase. Madhva's bhāṣya, in our source, has no comment on this verse.

parallels.quote: मृत्युप्रोक्तां नचिकेतोऽथ लब्ध्वा विद्यामेतां योगविधिं च कृत्स्नम्
parallels.note: The Kaṭha's last verses again name the teaching as told by Death and received by Naciketas.

contemporary.text: The verse honours two acts that keep a teaching alive: telling and hearing. A teaching that is only read in private is easily lost; one that is told and listened to is carried. Many learning traditions still rely on this. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: Is there a story you heard as a child that you would want to pass on? Why that one?
reflect.deeper: Why might a text praise its own telling and hearing at the end of a section?
reflect.practice: Retell the story of Naciketas so far, in your own words, to someone else or in writing.

flags.note: brahmaloka: Brahman itself (Śaṅkara), or the world of Brahmā; Raṅgarāmānuja does not discuss it. Madhva's bhāṣya has no comment on the verse.
